newsitem.title: INDIA: India seen offering 5-year trade curb phase-out.
newsitem.headline: India seen offering 5-year trade curb phase-out.

text.p: India is likely to offer to eliminate curbs on imports within five years after its trade partners rejected its proposal to phase out controls over seven years, trade analysts said on Wednesday.

Talks at the World Trade Organisation in Geneva ended in deadlock on Tuesday after India offered to phase out quantitative import restrictions such as quotas over a seven-year period, a Commerce Ministry spokeswoman said.
She said that after the meeting, during "informal" talks, India suggested a six-year timetable. But its trading partners demanded a maximum period of five years, she said.

"The developed countries wanted heavy frontloading of items in the time schedule with only very few items in the sixth year, even though on paper it would seem as though India had the benefit of six years to phase out," she said.

Last month, talks at the multilateral trade body on the proposed elimination of India's import restrictions were suspended after New Delhi's major trade partners objected to its initial plan to phase out curbs over nine years.

India then told the WTO Committee on Balance of Payments Restrictions it needed a phase-out period of nine years to avoid a sharp decline in foreign exchange reserves, which could trigger a balance of payments crisis.
But delegates said India's reserves no longer justified restrictions that reduced access to the vast Indian market, and called for a transitional period of two to three years.
India's foreign exchange reserves reached $28.83 billion in June, up from $21.77 billion one year earlier.

"Broadly, India's point was that in assessing the foreign exchange reserves of a developing country over the medium term, the requirements of development have to be taken into account," the Commerce Ministry spokeswoman said.

The Committee will now produce a report on the discussions for the WTO's ruling General Council, which has its next meeting on July 17. The major trading powers were expected to ask India again to drop the restrictions.

"We have been fairly reasonable in terms of trying to bring the period down. We knew fully well nobody would accept nine or seven years," said Charan Wadhva, trade analyst at the Centre for Policy Research, told Reuters.

"I would probably say five years seems reasonable. It is a bargaining situation," he said. "We want to enter APEC and approach ASEAN, and until we approach their tariff levels, it is a difficult compulsion."

India is a full dialogue partner of the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) and an observer at an Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) sub-group. New Delhi has pledged to align its tariffs with APEC nations' by 2010.
But India, which began dismantling decades of socialist controls on its economy in 1991, was still vulnerable to volatile capital outflows, Wadhva said.
Rajesh Chadha, analyst at the National Council for Applied Economic Research, said India's economy was strong enough to absorb a phase-out period as short as three years.

"Five years should be the upper limit," he added. "A three- to five-year period should be enough since domestic producers have already been given signals to align their production with international levels."

Diplomats in Geneva said it was likely the United States and the European Union would challenge India through the WTO's dispute settlement process. Indian officials privately said they were confident Delhi could brush back any challenge.

"I think there is a good chance of a settlement close to the Indian position in that case," Wadhva said, adding that many European nations have refused to remove strict curbs on agricultural goods imports until 2003.
